topic.name: Tangent Vectors and Tangent Lines to Curves

question.text: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+(2+t^3)\,\mathbf j+(1+t^2)\,\mathbf k$, find all points at which $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r(t)$ are parallel.
question.explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t)\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2+t^3)\,\mathbf j + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(1+t^2) \,\mathbf k \\[3pt] &= \mathbf i +\: 3t^2\,\mathbf j +\: 2t\,\mathbf k \end{align*}

The vectors $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value $t_0$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $\mathbf r(t_0) = c \, \mathbf r'(t_0).$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) &= c \, \mathbf r'(t) \\[3pt] t\,\mathbf i+(2+t^3)\,\mathbf j+(1+t^2)\,\mathbf k&=c(\mathbf i +\: 3t^2\,\mathbf j +\: 2t\,\mathbf k ). \end{align*}

Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf i, \mathbf j, $ and $\mathbf k$ gives:

\[ \begin{cases} t=c\\ 2+t^3=c(3t^2)\\ 1+t^2=c(2t) \end{cases} \]

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality gives

\begin{align} 2+t^3&=3t^3 \\[3pt] 2 & =2t^3 \\[3pt] t^3 &=1 \\[3pt] t &=1 \end{align}

This satisfies also the equation $1+t^2=c(2t).$ Therefore, $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf r'$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1. $

Finally, since \begin{align*} \mathbf r(1)&=\mathbf i+(2+1^3)\,\mathbf j+(1+1^2)\,\mathbf k\\[3pt] &=\mathbf i+3\,\mathbf j+2\,\mathbf k, \end{align*} we conclude that $\mathbf r(t)$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are parallel at the point $P(1,3,2).$

example.title: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector

question.text: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=(1-\sin{t})\,\mathbf i+(t+\cos{t})\,\mathbf j + 4\sin\left( \dfrac{t}{2}\right)\,\mathbf k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ valid for all real values of $u?$
question.explanation:
At the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the vector $\mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

\[ \mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )+u\mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ), \quad u \in (-\infty, \infty). \]

First, we find $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ) &=\left(1-\sin{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\right)\,\mathbf i+\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\cos{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\right)\,\mathbf j+ 4\sin\left( \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\,\mathbf k \\[3pt] &=(1-1)\mathbf i+\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+0\right)\,\mathbf j+ 2\sqrt{2}\,\mathbf k\\[3pt] &=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\,\mathbf j+ 2\sqrt{2}\,\mathbf k \end{align*}

Now, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(1-\sin{t})\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t+\cos{t})\,\mathbf j + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[4\sin\left( \dfrac{t}{2}\right)\right]\,\mathbf k \\[3pt] &= -\cos{t}\,\mathbf i + (1-\sin t) \,\mathbf j + 2\cos\left( \dfrac{t}{2}\right)\,\mathbf k \end{align*}

Then, we evaluate $\mathbf r'(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ) &=-\cos \dfrac{\pi}{2} \,\mathbf i + \left(1-\sin \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)\,\mathbf j+ 2\cos\left( \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\,\mathbf k \\[3pt] &=-0 \,\mathbf i + \left(1-1\right)\,\mathbf j + \sqrt{2}\,\mathbf k \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{2}\,\mathbf k \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is
\[ \mathbf R(u)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\,\mathbf j+ 2\sqrt{2}\,\mathbf k +u\left( \sqrt{2}\,\mathbf k \right), \quad u \in (-\infty, \infty). \]

example.title: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve

question.text: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t^2 - 1 , \arctan{t} \right\rangle$ at the point where $t = 0,$ valid for all real values of $u?$
question.explanation:
At the point where $t = 0,$ the vector $\mathbf r'(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as \[ \mathbf R(u) = \mathbf{r}(0) + u\mathbf r'(0), \quad u \in (-\infty, \infty) \]

First, we find $\mathbf r(0)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r(0) & = \left\langle 0^2 - 1 , \arctan{0} \right\rangle \\[3pt] & = \left\langle -1 , 0 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) & = \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}( t^2 - 1 ) , \, \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}( \arctan{t} )\right\rangle \\[5pt] & = \left\langle 2t , \dfrac{1}{t^2 + 1} \right\rangle \end{align*}

Then, we evaluate $\mathbf r'(t)$ at $t = 0 \mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(0) & = \left\langle 2(0) , \dfrac{1}{0^2 + 1} \right\rangle\\[5pt] & = \left\langle 0 , 1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t = 0$ is
\[ \mathbf R(u) = \left\langle -1 , 0 \right\rangle +u\left\langle 0, 1\right\rangle, \quad u \in (-\infty, \infty). \]

example.title: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve

question.text: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle 2t^3, 3t^2-6t\right\rangle,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $\left\langle 1, -4 \right\rangle.$
question.explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) & = \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}( 2t^3) , \, \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left( 3t^2 - 6t\right)\right\rangle\\[5pt] & = \left\langle 6t^2 , 6t - 6 \right\rangle \end{align*}

The vectors $\left\langle 1, -4\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $\left\langle 1 , -4\right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.$ So, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle 1 , -4\right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) & = 0 \\[5pt] \left\langle 1 , -4 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle 6t^2 , 6t - 6 \right\rangle & = 0 \\[5pt] 1(6t^2) + (-4)(6t-6) & = 0\\[5pt] 6t^2 - 24t + 24 & = 0\\[5pt] t^2 - 4t + 4 & = 0\\[5pt] (t-2)^2 & = 0\\[5pt] t & = 2. \end{align*}

Therefore, the only solution is $t = 2.$

Finally, since \begin{align*} \mathbf r(2) & = \left\langle 2(2)^3 , 3(2)^2 - 6(2)\right\rangle \\[5pt] & = \left\langle 16 , 0 \right\rangle, \end{align*} we conclude that $\left\langle 1 , -4\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $\left( 16, 0\right).$

example.title: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector

question.text: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=(1-3t)\,\mathbf i+2\sqrt{t}\,\mathbf j$, find all of the points at which $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r(t)$ are perpendicular.
question.explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(1-3t)\,\mathbf i+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left(2\sqrt{t}\right)\,\mathbf j \\[5pt] &=-3\,\mathbf i+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,\mathbf j \end{align*}

The vectors $\mathbf r(t)$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $\mathbf r(t) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) &= 0 \\[5pt] \left[ (1-3t)\,\mathbf i+2\sqrt{t}\,\mathbf j \right] \cdot \left( -3\mathbf i+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,\mathbf j \right) &= 0 \\[5pt] (1-3t) \cdot (-3)+ 2\sqrt{t} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{t}} &= 0 \\[5pt] -3 + 9t + 2 &= 0 \\[5pt] 9t - 1 &= 0. \end{align*}

Therefore, the only solution is $t=\dfrac{1}{9}.$

Finally, since

\begin{align*} \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right) = \left( 1- 3\cdot \dfrac{1}{9}\right)\,\mathbf i+2\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{9}}\,\mathbf j = \dfrac{2}{3}\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{2}{3}\,\mathbf j , \end{align*}

we conclude that $\mathbf r(t)$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$
